label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
**Thursdays on the tea trolley**

Bridget has asked me to write this month's piece, and I should say at the outset that she has a motive. The Thursday tea trolley in the day therapy unit is meant to be run by a rota of six. Since the summer there have been four of us. One of our number moved to Sheffield to be near her grandchildren and another is recovering from a knee operation, and neither of those is the sort of thing one can argue with. So we are two short, and I have been asked to see whether anyone reading this might fancy it.

I started in March 2022. I had retired eighteen months earlier after 41 years of bookkeeping, most of them for a builders' merchant in Dereham, and I had assumed retirement would arrange itself. It didn't. Most weeks I had no regular reason to leave the house, and I drifted. I mention this so that nobody imagines I turned up at the hospice out of nobility. I wanted somewhere to be on a Thursday.

I very nearly didn't come, because I thought what I suspect many of you think: that volunteering in a hospice must be either harrowing or terribly skilled. On the tea trolley, at any rate, it is neither.

The day unit sees between 14 and 18 patients on a Thursday. Many come for the art group or the hand massage, and a good few come simply for the company. Most go home afterwards. Anyone expecting hushed voices would be surprised by the din. It is a noisy and rather jolly place.

As for skill, you need no nursing knowledge whatever. You need to be able to push a trolley, remember who takes what, and listen. Four decades of keeping ledgers straight have turned out to be handy for the remembering. The listening I am still learning. Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars and tells me about the 1953 floods every week, slightly differently each time. I used to correct the dates. I have stopped.

Nor do you need to be good at it straight away. In my first week I tipped an entire jug of milk over the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so much she had to be given a tissue, and told me it was the best afternoon she'd had in a month. I have not been as entertaining since.

The other thing I can pass on is that the bourbon biscuits always go first. We now hide a packet for the late group.

I won't pretend every Thursday is cheerful. Some weeks are hard, and there are afternoons when someone you had got used to seeing isn't there. When that happens the staff look after the volunteers as well as everyone else, and nobody is left to manage on their own. Those days are the exception, though, and I have never once driven home wishing I hadn't gone.

Now the particulars. The trolley runs from 1.30 to 4pm, and the commitment is one Thursday a fortnight. Before you start, Bridget takes you through an induction, which lasts about two hours. There is also a short food hygiene course to do online, which the hospice pays for. That is the whole of it.

If you are even slightly curious, there is a volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room. There will be tea and biscuits and no obligation of any kind. I shall be there and will happily answer questions, including ones about the milk. If you can't manage that date, ring Bridget on the volunteering line and she will tell you anything you want to know.

We need two people. I'd be content, for now, with two of you coming to have a look.

---

Two things to check before it goes up:

- **Patient names:** I've used Mr Hollis and Pat as you gave them. Bridget may want them changed or their permission sought, since the blog is public.
- **Phone number:** I haven't put in a number for the volunteering line, as you didn't give one, so that needs adding.
